name: Femi Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a senior field researcher at the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy phone cables, chargers, cases and small speakers for Brightwire Distribution, which sells to about four hundred independent shops. Mornings are supplier calls with factories at the other end of the world, so I'm up early for the time difference. Afternoons I'm in a spreadsheet tool I wrote myself that scores suppliers on price, delay history and defect rates.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being the person who spots a trend six weeks early, like the month everybody suddenly wanted braided cables. What wears me out is the pace: a container delayed at a port can wreck a quarter. I live alone in a one-bedroom flat and send some money to my mum every month, so I keep a close eye on my cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's overhyped but still handy. At work I'd say it clears maybe four hours of boring work a week, and that's real, just not a revolution. Online I'd probably post a screenshot of a supplier-scoring script and a joke about the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's mostly good for me. If AI stays a tool, then someone who uses it every day stays ahead of colleagues who don't. The thing nagging me is the money I send my mum and that my rent keeps rising faster than my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and keep tinkering. I'd probably finish the supplier-risk dashboard, because Brightwire would pay for the time it saves. And I'd raise my savings from two months to four, which a plateau gives me the calm to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit smug, honestly. I get to keep my edge without anything changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. What does a plateau do to your edge at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes my edge a bit smaller, because if everybody catches up the gap shrinks. But a plateau means they catch up slowly, so I get a few more years of being the guy who knows how to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a pressure you carry that has nothing to do with AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money for my mum, mostly. She's got a small pension. I cover my mum's electricity and a few other bills, so if I lost a month of pay it would hit her as well as me.

say: It's **overhyped but handy**: it clears about four boring hours a week, and I'd joke about it online.
I'd post a screenshot of my **supplier-scoring script**.
think: If AI stays a tool, using it **every day** keeps me ahead of colleagues who don't.
Rising **rent** and the money I send my mum nag at me more than AI does.
do: Finish the **supplier-risk dashboard**, which Brightwire would pay for because it saves time.
Raise savings from **two months to four**.
feel: **Calm** and a little smug, keeping my edge while nothing much changes.
S0.quote: I cover my mum's electricity and a few other bills, so if I lost a month of pay it would hit her as well as me.
fieldNote: Femi is calm because AI gives him an **edge** if it stays a tool, and his real pressure is family money.
He names **supporting his mother** as the thing that makes any lost month matter.

steps.text: Finish the supplier-risk dashboard and show it to the buying director
Raise savings from two months of costs to four
Keep running the weekly supplier scoring and trend spotting by hand

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the one to get ready for, and I'd say it to my team. At work I'd show people how I use the tools and offer a lunchtime session. Online I'd argue that the gains should be shared and not just land with shareholders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm a bit excited and a bit nervous. My own work is mostly thinking tasks, so some of it will go. But I'm the one who builds the tools, so I'd likely be one of the people running the new setup rather than replaced by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to lead an AI purchasing project at Brightwire and make myself the person who owns it. I'd also pick up a course on data and supply chain analytics. And I'd start a small side project, selling a supplier-checking tool to other distributors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Energised, with a hint of dread. I like that I'm ahead, but I know ahead only lasts until the next update.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your own tasks does the software take, and which stay yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Routine reorders, price comparison and delay prediction go to software. What stays mine is deciding which supplier to risk on a new product, because that's a judgement call with money on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you worry the juniors won't get the chance you got?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that bothers me. I learned the job by sitting next to a senior buyer, and if software does the entry-level work then juniors won't have a seat to sit in. I'd push to keep a few trainee roles, even if it costs a bit.

say: This is the one to **get ready for**; I'd run a lunchtime session showing the team how I use the tools.
The gains should be **shared**, not only land with shareholders.
think: Some of my thinking work will go, but I build the tools, so I'd likely **run the new setup**.
Staying ahead only lasts **until the next update**.
do: Offer to **lead an AI project** at Brightwire and own it.
Take a **supply-chain analytics** course and prototype a supplier-checking tool to sell elsewhere.
feel: **Energised** with a hint of dread, since being ahead only lasts so long.
S1.quote: I learned the job by sitting next to a senior buyer, and if software does the entry-level work then juniors won't have a seat to sit in.
fieldNote: Femi treats Steady Disruption as an **opening**, and moves first to own the project.
His worry is for **juniors** who lose the apprentice-style seat he learned in.

steps.text: Pitch an AI purchasing project to the buying director and lead it
Run a lunchtime session showing the team my scoring tool
Build a supplier-checking tool to pilot with two other distributors
Start an evening course in supply-chain analytics

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules now: licensing for the biggest systems, a payment into a public fund and a pause on mass layoffs while we sort it out. I'd say it at work, to friends, and in a letter to whoever represents me. Two years is wildly short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm scared. If AI does any thinking work better and cheaper, buying is exactly what goes, and being ahead of colleagues won't matter because the whole desk goes together. My mum depends on me, so a job loss isn't just my problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard from the first week, get my cushion to six months and look at how to turn my skills into something owned by me, a small consultancy or a tool. I'd also join the union branch and back any local campaign for retraining pay. And I'd talk with my mum about what we cut if I'm out of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, with a streak of excitement that I'm a bit ashamed of. It's a huge thing happening and I'd be watching it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If everything arrives in two years, is being ahead of colleagues still worth something?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being ahead is worth something for a year, maybe two. After that the machine is ahead of both of us. What matters is whether I own a bit of it, or work with the people who do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should be responsible for people who aren't ahead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government and the companies that make the systems. I don't accept that this is an individual's problem, and I'll say so even if it makes me sound like a broken record.

say: We need **rules now**: licensing, a public fund and a pause on mass layoffs while we sort it out.
I'd write to my **representative** and say two years is wildly short.
think: Buying is exactly what goes, and being ahead won't help because the **whole desk goes**.
My mum depends on me, so a job loss is **not only mine**.
do: Save hard and get my cushion to **six months**, then turn my skills into something I own.
Join the **union branch** and back local campaigns for retraining pay.
feel: **Scared**, with a streak of excitement I'm a bit ashamed of.
S2.quote: Being ahead is worth something for a year, maybe two. After that the machine is ahead of both of us.
fieldNote: Femi's confidence is **thin** here: his daily AI use doesn't protect him if the whole desk goes.
He aims to **own** a piece of the change, which is his adaptive reflex under stress.

steps.text: Build the cushion to six months of costs within the first year
Launch a small supplier-risk consultancy for independent distributors
Join the union branch and attend the retraining campaign
Write to my representative demanding licensing and a public fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the same deal but we're not helpless. At work I'd push for an early plan and say we could use these years to train people. Online I'd campaign a bit for retraining accounts, paid for by the firms who gain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's the best scenario for someone like me. By thirty-two I could have built something of my own, or moved into a role that uses people skills, and I'd have savings. My real risk is complacency, thinking I'm adaptive so I'm fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get a certificate in supply-chain risk and start the side tool as a real business, even if it earns only a bit. I'd keep a six-month cushion. And I'd look at product-sourcing work that involves visiting factories, which stays human for longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but optimistic. It feels like standing at the edge of a swimming pool you know you'll have to jump into, with a few years of warm-up first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently with five years than with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years it's a scramble. With five, I can build a business that makes money before the thinking part of my job disappears. I'd have a track record, customers and maybe a small team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the delay for robots matter for someone who sits at a desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Visiting factories and checking a batch with my own eyes isn't something software can do for three more years. But I wouldn't plan my life around that gap, because it's closing fast too.

say: It's the same deal but we're **not helpless**; I'd push for an early plan to train people.
I'd campaign for **retraining accounts** paid by the firms who gain.
think: This is the best case for someone like me: by thirty-two I could have **built something**.
My real risk is **complacency**, thinking I'm adaptive so I'm fine.
do: Get a **supply-chain risk** certificate and turn the side tool into a real business.
Keep a **six-month cushion** and look at factory-visit sourcing work.
feel: **Uneasy but optimistic**, like standing at a pool's edge with some warm-up time.
S3.quote: With two years it's a scramble. With five, I can build a business that makes money before the thinking part of my job disappears.
fieldNote: Femi sees five years as enough to **earn from his tool** before desk buying goes.
He names **complacency** as his own weak spot, which shows self-awareness.

steps.text: Earn a supply-chain risk certificate in the first year
Turn the supplier tool into a registered business with paying customers
Hold a six-month cushion while the business grows
Apply for sourcing roles that involve visiting factories in person

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a great chance if people use it. At work I'd say let's plan jobs for 2036 and not wait. Online I'd argue for a basic shared dividend, since the machines will be making money for somebody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm quite relaxed. At thirty-seven I'd have had a decade to move into something owned or something human. Even if buying vanishes, I'd have another set of skills and savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI daily, build the business slowly and maybe invest in a small share of a distributor. I'd save for a flat, since renting forever isn't great. And I'd help my mum pay for her house repairs now while she's still around to enjoy them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and hopeful. Most of my worry is about other people, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what changes for your mum and for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For my mum, ten years means she'd be seventy-five and I'd be comfortable enough to cover her costs. For me it means I can try, fail at a business once, and still recover. That's the value of ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a long runway tempt you to relax?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, and that's the trap. I'd set myself a rule: one big change every two years, so I never drift.

say: It's a great chance if people use it: let's **plan jobs for 2036** now.
I'd argue for a **shared dividend**, since machines will make money for somebody.
think: At thirty-seven I'd have had a decade to move into something **owned or human**.
Most of my worry is for **other people**, not me.
do: Keep using AI daily and build the **side business** slowly while saving for a flat.
Help my mum pay for **house repairs** now.
feel: **Calm and hopeful**, with the worry pointed at other people.
S4.quote: For me it means I can try, fail at a business once, and still recover.
fieldNote: Femi is calm because ten years lets him **fail once and recover**, which fits his comfort with risk.
He sets himself a **rule** of one big change every two years to avoid drifting.

steps.text: Keep using AI daily and build the sourcing tool into a paid service
Run the consultancy on evenings and grow to five customers
Save for a flat deposit within six years
Pay for repairs to my mum's house now

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, 2028. I'd be at the start of my career with a mum who depends on me and a desk job that goes first. What would help is rules that make companies share gains, plus paid retraining and some way to own a part of what the machines earn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that being good with AI doesn't make me safe, and I'd like people to stop assuming it does. I'm adaptable, not immune.

portrait: Femi is a **27-year-old senior buyer** of phone accessories who uses AI every day and wrote his own supplier-scoring tool.
He lives alone and sends **money to his mum** each month, which is what makes job loss matter.
He is progressive, wants **shared gains and regulation**, and blames the firms that profit from the change.
His mood runs from **calm** to **alarmed** at the two-year mark, and returns to calm with ten years.
He moves first: **side business**, courses and projects he owns.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture**: a desk job that goes first and a mother who depends on his pay.
whatWouldHelp: **Rules** that make companies share gains, paid retraining and a way to own part of what machines earn.
